newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Mrs. Clinton says Chelsea a help on Africa tour.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton says Chelsea a help on Africa tour.

text.p: U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton said on Thursday she hoped that bringing her daughter Chelsea along on her Africa tour "might plant a seed" for improving the health care and education of African girls.

At a news conference in the tranquil setting of Serengeti, a protected habitat for East Africa's varied wildlife in Tanzania, President Bill Clinton's wife was asked about the impact her 17-year-old daughter was having on the people they have seen in small villages during their six-nation tour of Africa.

"All of a sudden you may have some woman somewhere say, 'Well, I'm going to send my daughter to school,' or 'No, my daughter is going to get the health care she needs,' or 'This village is going to have a school for girls,'" Mrs. Clinton said.
Interest in the first daughter has intensified after Chelsea, always closely guarded from the press by her parents, on Tuesday talked publicly about serious subjects for the first time.

Her message about social problems among American youth and how they might be cured caused reporters travelling with the Clintons to essentially drop everything and work on stories about the teenager. This caused not a small amount of concern among Mrs. Clinton and her aides.

Mrs. Clinton was initially wary about discussing her daughter while talking to reporters after a long, dusty drive from Tanzania's Ngorongoro Crater, its fossil-rich Olduvai Gorge, and through the flat plain of the Serengeti, where the Clintons saw giraffes, cheetahs and other creatures.
Asked what Chelsea's impressions had been on the trip, Mrs. Clinton simply said: "She's had a wonderful time."
But she warmed to the topic later, saying Chelsea's participation in the first lady's foreign travel had been beneficial.

She said that based on a similar experience in taking Chelsea along with her on a trip to Southeast Asia two years ago, some awareness might have surfaced there that "in our country we value our girls and our boys, that the president of the United States has one child, it happens to be a girl, and he's invested in her education and is proud of her."

"And I think that those of us who are lucky enough to be women at a time when we've had so many advantages because of families and societies that nurtured us along, any time we get a chance to exemplify those opportunities to other women, it might plant a seed," Mrs. Clinton said.

The Clintons later flew from the Serengeti in northern Tanzania to Kampala, Uganda, where the motorcade route into the city from Entebbe airport was lined with thousands of Ugandans, often four-deep along the road.

Chelsea, who is soon to learn which universities have accepted her for enrollment next fall, has been a constant companion to her mother on this two-week tour and from all appearances has shown herself to be mature, respectful of other cultures and inquisitive about them.

Indeed, the comments that caused the U.S. television networks to plan stories on her for Thursday night -- the first day videotape from Chelsea's comments could be sent back to America because of the remote locale -- were essentially the same message that her parents have given in countless speeches.

In Arusha, Tanzania, Mrs. Clinton volunteered Chelsea to answer questions from teenaged girls who had recently climbed Mount Kilimanjaro because they were about the same age and Chelsea, as a hiker, could relate to them better.

Asked what obstacles young people face in America, Chelsea talked of a "hopelessness and cynicism" that grips many because of a culture of drugs and violence. She said adults can only do so much and that it is up to the young people themselves to reverse this downward spiral.

During the visit to the Olduvai Gorge, where many artifacts from early humans have been unearthed, Mrs. Clinton was shown examples of petrified fossils found at the site and said it proved the usefulness of public and private investment in learning more about human evolution.
